result.summary: Pausanias gives rival traditions about the earliest town at Delphi, its founders, and how it got the names Lycorea, Delphi and Pytho. He ends with a tale of an insolent son of Crius who plundered the temple and was foretold a punishing arrow by Phemonoe.

scenes.title: Parnassus founds the first town
scenes.summary: Parnassus, son of a Nymph and of two fathers, builds the oldest town. It is destroyed in Deucalion's flood, and survivors follow wolves up the mountain and found Lycorea.
scenes.stakes: Survivors of the flood must escape destruction by water.

scenes.title: Rival origins of Delphi's name
scenes.summary: Other traditions name Lycorus, Delphus and Thyia as founders or namesakes. The town is also called Pytho, perhaps after Pythes.

scenes.title: The dragon rots at Pytho
scenes.summary: The common tradition says Apollo's arrows killed the dragon set by Earth to guard her oracle, and it rotted there, giving Pytho its name.
scenes.stakes: The dragon guards Earth's oracle against Apollo.

scenes.title: Phemonoe's oracle on the plunderer
scenes.summary: Crius's insolent son plunders the temple and rich houses. The Delphians beg Apollo for help and Phemonoe prophesies his punishment.
scenes.stakes: The Delphians risk a second plundering of the temple and their homes.

alias_notes.explanation: Epithet of Apollo used in the oracle.
Older or alternative name of the town, explained by rotting or by Pythes.

notable_quotes.reason: The hexameter oracle of Phemonoe foretelling Apollo's arrow and purification by Cretans.

analysis.text: Pausanias lists competing local traditions about Delphi's origins, showing how names were explained by genealogy and myth.
The passage shows how Greek sites justified their names and sanctity through heroic ancestry and appeals to Homer.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says Pytho comes from the Greek word for rotting, a folk etymology tied to the slain dragon.

language_notes.text: "Two fathers": a hero was held to have a divine father and a mortal one, so his birth carried both divine and human status.
Deucalion's flood is the Greek great flood; Deucalion and Pyrrha survived it on a ship and repopulated the earth.
Autochthon means "sprung from the land itself", a native rather than an immigrant.
Orgies here means ecstatic religious rites of Dionysus, not the modern sense. Thyiades were his frenzied female worshippers.
Homer's Catalogue of the Phocians is the list of Phocian contingents in the Iliad, Book 2, which names Pytho.
"Make genealogies about everything" is mildly scornful: Pausanias doubts those who invent a founding ancestor for every place name.
Homer's Sirens, in the Odyssey, lured sailors with song; their island was heaped with the rotting bones of the men who listened.
The Cretans purifying Apollo refers to his purification after killing the dragon, with Cretans linked to the founding of his Delphic cult.
"Devours Parnassus" means plunders the sacred mountain's treasures; Phœbus is a title of Apollo.

context_notes.text: Poseidon is the Greek sea god, also linked to earthquakes and horses.
The Corycian cavern is a large cave on Parnassus, sacred to Pan and the Nymphs.
Phemonoe was reputed to be the first Pythia, Apollo's prophetess at Delphi, and the inventor of hexameter verse.

literary_notes.text: The story explains the name Lycorea by the wolves the survivors followed, a typical origin tale for a place name.
Pausanias cites Homer's rotting sailors to support the etymology, using literary authority as evidence.
The oracle announces the plunderer's coming punishment and Apollo's lasting fame, preparing the reader for the outcome.
